note: Read 2026-10-31. Majority is each state's own law; no federal or uniform source sets one, so the country's majority is null and every state is held in 'regions' from its own code. Read today and held at 18, each from the legislature's own published code (the sections are named in the sources): Arizona, Colorado, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Florida, Iowa, Idaho, Kansas, Massachusetts, Maryland, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Montana, North Carolina, North Dakota, Nevada, Ohio, Oregon, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Utah, Texas, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, West Virginia and Wyoming. Where the section read is the code's general definition of adult or minor (Arizona, Maine, Minnesota, Virginia) it is held as the majority; Colorado's § 13-22-101 sets full age at eighteen for contracts and other listed purposes. Marriage ending minority (Iowa, Utah, Oregon, Kansas at sixteen) isn't held. Null, not read today (the blocker file names each attempt): Alaska, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Georgia, Hawaii, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Missouri, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Wisconsin. Alabama: Code of Alabama 1975, § 26-1-1 (Acts 1975 No. 77, last Act 2019-447), read through the Legislature's own code service (alison.legislature.state.al.us, its GraphQL source): a person is relieved of the disabilities of minority at nineteen. Mississippi: Miss. Code § 1-3-27 defines a minor as under twenty-one; the Code itself is published only through LexisNexis and wasn't read. The Legislature's own pages show the rule as it stands: House Bill 277 of the 2026 Regular Session, 'An act to lower the age of majority from twenty-one to eighteen', would have amended § 1-3-21 ('infant', under twenty-one) and others, and died in committee on 3 February 2026; so twenty-one holds. Nebraska: Neb. Rev. Stat. § 43-2101 (last Laws 2019, LB55): everyone under nineteen is a minor, and marriage ends minority; but as it now reads a person of eighteen or more who isn't a ward of the state may enter a binding contract or lease and sign notes and security instruments in their own name. Held at 19, the minority; the contracting age of eighteen isn't held. Emancipation by marriage (Alabama, Nebraska) isn't held. Work: Fair Labor Standards Act, as the Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division states it (Fact Sheet #43, revised December 2016): sixteen is the basic minimum age for employment; fourteen and fifteen may work outside school hours in limited non-hazardous jobs and hours (not held); eighteen for the hazardous occupations; under fourteen only work exempt from the Act, such as acting. Performers: the FLSA exempts children employed as actors or performers (29 U.S.C. § 213(c)(3), not read today; the Fact Sheet's 'such as ... acting'), so 'free' federally. Most states require their own entertainment work permit for a minor (California's Entertainment Work Permit, New York's Child Performer Permit, and others); the form holds no state work rule, so the state permits aren't held. State laws may also set stricter minimum ages. Service: none; there is no draft. The Military Selective Service Act (50 U.S.C. § 3802) makes every male citizen and male resident between eighteen and twenty-six register with the Selective Service System, a duty the form doesn't hold.

sources.title: Fact Sheet #43: Child Labor Provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) for Nonagricultural Occupations, U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division (revised December 2016)
sources.said: Basic minimum age for employment. Sixteen- and 17-year-olds may be employed for unlimited hours in any occupation other than those declared hazardous by the Secretary of Labor. ... Children under 14 years of age may not be employed in non-agricultural occupations covered by the FLSA. Permissible employment for such children is limited to work that is exempt from the FLSA (such as delivering newspapers to the consumer and acting).
